questions.title: Does NF4 rescale by standard deviation or by absolute max during quantization?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the QLoRA paper and I'm confused about the normalization step for NF4. In the NF4 paragraph, they say weights are transformed into the range $[-1,1]$ and mention matching the standard deviation of the data type, but the concrete procedure for block-wise quantization earlier uses absolute max rescaling. For NF4 specifically, do they normalize each block by $\text{absmax}$ (as in Eq. 1), or by an estimate of $\sigma$ to match the $N(0,1)$ quantiles? If it is $\text{absmax}$ per block for step (3), how does that remain "information-theoretically optimal" for a normal distribution whose tails vary block-to-block?

questions.title: How exactly are the NF4 codebook values computed and why is it ‘information-theoretically optimal’?
questions.question_body: The paper defines NF4 by taking mid-quantiles of $N(0,1)$: $q_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(Q_X(\tfrac{i}{2^k+1}) + Q_X(\tfrac{i+1}{2^k+1})\big)$ and then normalizing to $[-1,1]$. 1) Why take midpoints between adjacent quantiles rather than the quantile boundaries themselves? 2) In what precise sense is this "information-theoretically optimal" for zero-mean Gaussians—does it minimize expected quantization error under $N(0,1)$, or maximize entropy of bin occupancy, or both? 3) How does the asymmetric construction to include an exact zero (splitting positive/negative bins) affect optimality guarantees?

questions.title: What does “Double Quantization” quantize, and is it different from quantizing weights twice?
questions.question_body: Section Double Quantization says they quantize the quantization constants $c_2^{\text{FP32}}$ into $c_2^{\text{FP8}}$ with a second level constant $c_1^{\text{FP32}}$. I first thought this meant weights themselves get quantized twice. Can someone confirm the exact pipeline? As I understand it: weights $\mathbf{W}$ are quantized into $\mathbf{W}^{\text{NF4}}$ using per-block scales $c_2$; then $c_2$ values are themselves block-quantized to FP8 with their own per-block scale $c_1$. At runtime, you dequantize $c_2$ via $c_1$, then dequantize $\mathbf{W}$ via the recovered $c_2$. Is that correct? Are there any numerical stability issues from dequantizing a dequantized scale?

questions.title: Deriving the memory savings of Double Quantization: where does the 0.373 bits/parameter come from?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that with blocksize 64 for weights and 256 for the $c_2$ scales, the memory for scales drops from $\tfrac{32}{64}=0.5$ bits/parameter to $\tfrac{8}{64} + \tfrac{32}{64\cdot256}=0.127$ bits/parameter, a 0.373 bpp reduction. Could someone walk through the calculation assumptions? In particular: 1) Are we assuming 32-bit storage for $c_1$ and 8-bit for quantized $c_2$? 2) Why is there no extra overhead for per-block offsets (they subtract mean before quantizing $c_2$)? 3) Is metadata (like block headers) ignored, or amortized to negligible cost?

questions.title: Why choose blocksize 64 for weights and 256 for $c_2$ scales in QLoRA?
questions.question_body: Block-wise quantization trades off precision and scale-overhead. QLoRA uses blocksize 64 for $\mathbf{W}$ and 256 for the scale quantization $c_2$. How sensitive are results to these choices? Is 64 the smallest block size that avoids large outlier-induced distortion under NF4, or is it an empirical sweet spot? Are there results or heuristics linking model width, activation statistics, or outlier prevalence to an optimal blocksize?

questions.title: How do gradients flow through quantized weights if we never compute $\partial E / \partial \mathbf{W}$?
questions.question_body: The paper says only LoRA adapter gradients $\partial E/\partial \mathbf{L}_i$ are needed and not $\partial E/\partial \mathbf{W}$ for the 4-bit base weights. But they also note that computing $\partial E/\partial \mathbf{L}_i$ entails computing $\partial \mathbf{X}/\partial \mathbf{W}$ with dequantized $\mathbf{W}^{\text{BF16}}$. Can someone outline the backward pass math? Do we treat $\mathbf{W}$ as a constant in the update sense (no optimizer state), but still use it in Jacobian-vector products to propagate gradients to $\mathbf{L}_i$? Is any straight-through estimator (STE) used for the quantization nonlinearity, or is quantization only in storage and all computed tensors are differentiable BF16?

questions.title: Is there a mismatch between the NF4 ‘optimal for Gaussian’ claim and using absmax normalization per block?
questions.question_body: NF4’s codebook is built for $N(0,1)$, but blocks are normalized by absolute max rather than by variance. For heavy-tailed or skewed blocks, $\text{absmax}$ can be dominated by outliers, leaving most mass compressed near zero. Wouldn’t per-block standard-deviation scaling be more aligned with the Gaussian-optimized codebook? Is there empirical evidence that absmax performs better in practice for pretrained LLM weights with near-Gaussian but not exact normal distributions?

questions.title: What exactly is stored in memory during QLoRA training, and where are the savings coming from?
questions.question_body: In the Memory Requirement section, the paper says the 4-bit base model is about 5,048 MB for LLaMA-7B and that LoRA gradients can dominate memory without gradient checkpointing. Could someone provide a precise breakdown for a single transformer layer during training with QLoRA? Specifically: 1) storage for quantized weights $\mathbf{W}^{\text{NF4}}$, 2) storage for quantization constants with double quantization ($c_1$, $c_2$), 3) dequantized temporary BF16 weights during forward/backward, 4) activations and activation gradients with gradient checkpointing, 5) optimizer states for LoRA (paged) vs. full-model? Which of these scale with sequence length vs. parameter count?

questions.title: Why do default LoRA placements (Q and V only) fail to match 16-bit full finetuning?
questions.question_body: The paper finds that applying LoRA only to the attention Q and V projections underperforms, and that placing adapters in all linear layers is critical to match full finetuning. Is there an explanation for why limiting adaptation to Q/V is insufficient for instruction tuning? Do certain components (like output projections, feed-forward layers, or key/value) carry task-specific adjustments that cannot be captured by modifying attention projections alone? Any ablations quantifying which additional layers contribute most to the gap closing?

questions.title: Does QLoRA dequantize weights on-the-fly for every forward pass and what is the runtime cost?
questions.question_body: Implementation-wise, QLoRA stores weights in NF4 and dequantizes to BF16 for matrix multiplications. Is dequantization performed on-the-fly every forward/backward pass, or are there caches at the block level? How much overhead does double dequantization (first recovering $c_2$ from $c_1$, then weights from $c_2$) add relative to 16-bit inference/training? The paper says there is no runtime degradation vs 16-bit full finetuning—do they have microbenchmarks showing dequant cost is negligible compared to GEMMs at large batch/sequence sizes?

questions.title: What failure mode do Paged Optimizers address, and when would paging slow training?
questions.question_body: Paged Optimizers rely on CUDA unified memory to page optimizer states between GPU and CPU RAM when long sequences cause transient spikes. 1) Which tensors are paged (optimizer states for LoRA only, or also intermediate grads)? 2) What pattern of sequence lengths or batch accumulation causes spikes large enough to need paging? 3) Is there a threshold of host-GPU bandwidth or page fault rate beyond which training slows significantly? Any guidance on how to monitor paging events and tune batch/sequence length to avoid stalls?

questions.title: How does NF4 handle exact zeros and does the asymmetric binning change reconstruction bias?
questions.question_body: To get an exact zero, the paper proposes asymmetric NF4: $2^{k-1}$ negative bins and $2^{k-1}+1$ positive bins, then removing one duplicate zero. How does this affect the mean of the reconstructed values when the true distribution is symmetric around zero? Is there a slight positive bias due to the extra positive bin density near zero, or does the removal of one zero value ensure symmetry in practice? Any quantitative comparison of reconstruction bias vs. symmetric quantizers that include a zero code explicitly?

questions.title: Clarifying the notation: is ‘BrainFloat16’ in the text a typo for ‘BFloat16’?
questions.question_body: In the QLoRA definition and summary, the paper alternates between “BFloat16” and “BrainFloat” (e.g., “16-bit BrainFloat”). Is this just a typo or colloquial term for the standard BF16 format? There is no separate ‘BrainFloat’ format that differs from BF16 in this context, right?

questions.title: How do they ensure that 4-bit QLoRA ‘recovers’ 16-bit performance without overfitting to the finetune data?
questions.question_body: The results show NF4 QLoRA matches 16-bit full finetuning and 16-bit LoRA on GLUE, TK-Instruct, and MMLU in their setups. Could this parity be partly due to overfitting to the finetuning distribution that is then measured on similar tasks? Did the authors evaluate cross-task generalization where the test distribution is notably different from the finetune data? Any signs that 4-bit models are less robust out-of-domain than 16-bit, even if in-domain metrics match?

questions.title: Why does NF4 outperform FP4 and Int4 empirically if all are 4-bit quantizers?
questions.question_body: The paper reports NF4 significantly outperforming FP4 and Int4 across multiple models and tasks. Intuitively, I would expect FP4 to be more flexible due to exponent/mantissa, and Int4 to be simple but robust with per-block scaling. What property of the NF4 codebook gives it a consistent advantage? Is it primarily the equal-probability binning under Gaussian assumptions (reducing overload and granular distortion), or the inclusion of an exact zero, or interactions with dequantization in BF16 GEMMs?

questions.title: How do LoRA rank and scaling hyperparameters interact with placing adapters in every layer?
questions.question_body: The paper states that the projection rank $r$ did not matter much, while putting LoRA in more places did. Is there a known regime where increasing $r$ within a layer materially helps once adapters are in every linear submodule? Conversely, can we reduce $r$ and still match 16-bit if we keep full coverage across layers? Any guidance on the trade-off curve between number of adapter locations and per-adapter rank to keep memory roughly constant?

questions.title: What is the precise Elo setup and how sensitive are rankings to sampling and K?
questions.question_body: For chatbot evaluation, they compute Elo by sampling labeled pairwise comparisons 10,000 times and using $K=32$. 1) What is the exact update formula they use for Elo after each comparison (win/loss/tie handling)? 2) How sensitive are system-level Elo scores to the random sampling order, choice of $K$, and tie policy? 3) Could a subset of strong-vs-weak matches inflate a model’s Elo if not balanced across opponent strengths? Are there published confidence intervals or bootstrapped CIs per model?

questions.title: Is there any interaction between NF4 quantization and attention key/value cache precision at inference?
questions.question_body: During generation, attention KV caches can dominate memory and may be stored in lower precision. QLoRA focuses on training-time memory and quantized weights, but what precision is used for KV caches in their inference experiments for Guanaco models? If KV caches use FP16/BF16, could some of the observed parity with 16-bit finetuning be sensitive to inference-time cache precision rather than just weight quantization?

questions.title: How is bias handled: are bias terms stored/updated in 16-bit or quantized with NF4?
questions.question_body: The paper focuses on quantizing weight matrices and adding LoRA adapters. What about bias vectors in linear layers and layernorm parameters? Are they kept in BF16/FP16 and updated, frozen, or quantized to NF4? If biases remain in higher precision while weights are NF4, could that explain part of the performance parity with 16-bit full finetuning?

questions.title: Could 3-bit base weights with LoRA finetuning match 16-bit, or does NF4 rely on a 4-bit floor?
questions.question_body: The authors note as future work whether more aggressive quantization (e.g., 3-bit GPTQ + LoRA) might still recover 16-bit finetuning performance. Given the NF4 construction depends on $2^k$ quantiles, what pitfalls arise at $k=3$? Would outliers and block absmax scaling make 3-bit bins too coarse even with LoRA adaptation? Any preliminary results on perplexity or zero-shot accuracy drops when going from 4-bit to 3-bit with adapter finetuning?

questions.title: Do the per-block scales $c_2$ use absolute max or some robust statistic, and how are they quantized?
questions.question_body: For the first-level quantization of $\mathbf{W}$ into NF4, the paper mentions rescaling by absolute max per block, yielding scales $c_2^{\text{FP32}}$. Before double quantization, do they apply any clipping or robust estimation (like percentile-based scaling) to reduce sensitivity to single outliers? When quantizing $c_2$ to FP8 using blocks of 256, do they use absolute max again or a different procedure due to $c_2$ being strictly positive? They mention subtracting the mean to center around zero—does this imply a symmetric FP8 representation, and does mean subtraction introduce bias on dequant?
